transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-15
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE); Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE); Sam Ortiz (CTO, Stellaris Health); Jordan Lee (ML Engineer); Maya Patel (PM)

Auto-generated sections (partial):
- Topics: migration, dedicated vs hosted, benchmarking, security
- Action Items: see metadata

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for jumping on. I'm Alex from Redwood, I own the account here. With me is Priya our systems SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Sam: Hey Alex yeah doing well, thanks. Jordan and Maya are here with me. We're excited to dig in.
[00:10] Maya: Hi all, quick agenda from our side: we want to understand gaps from our OpenAI setup, what Dedicated buys us, and what the migration effort looks like.
[00:18] Priya: Great. High level from Redwood: Dedicated means reserved GPU capacity, private networking options, and more control over model versions and rollout policies. You keep a consistent API surface so your app changes are minimal in most cases.
[00:29] Jordan: When you say "consistent API" do you mean our current OpenAI calls will map 1:1, or will we have to change prompts or wrapper logic?
[00:35] Alex: For the most part you can keep the same call patterns — text generation, chat, embeddings — but there are model differences. We maintain a model catalog and compatibility layers: e.g., GPT-type models map cleanly, but smaller implementation differences exist with Anthropic-style safety layers.
[00:51] Jordan: Our main concerns are eval parity and latency. We have a couple of prompt sets where outputs must match or be within tolerance for clinical triage. We currently run on OpenAI and occasionally run with vLLM internally for some experiments. How do you approach parity?
[01:05] Priya: We typically do a benchmark workflow: you give us a representative prompt set and expected outputs or evaluation metrics. We run against the same model variants on our Dedicated infra and measure token-level latency, throughput, and scoring metrics. We also surface any distributional changes. We can run both the OpenAI equivalent model and an open model variant (e.g., Llama-family or other HF checkpoints) and provide a diff.
[01:24] Sam: Do you support Anthropic's Claude models or is it just GPT-family?
[01:29] Alex: We don't host Anthropic proprietary models, but we do support migration from Anthropic in terms of interface and offer comparable open models. If you need Anthropic specifically, we'd discuss a hybrid approach or continue using their hosted endpoints and route via smart routing.
[01:42] Jordan: You mentioned vLLM and TGI — is Redwood running its own vLLM-based runtime or do you integrate with these?
[01:49] Priya: Our serving runtime is a GPU-optimized engine with attention kernels and KV cache management that can run model variants compiled similarly to vLLM/TGI. We do support customer-provided runtimes in some Private cases, but for Dedicated we use our runtime tuned for throughput and latency. In the bench we compare parity vs vLLM/TGI to ensure scores align.
[02:09] Maya: On the infra side we need VPC peering and KMS integration, plus audit logs for compliance. Can you do SSO and RBAC?
[02:16] Alex: Yes. Dedicated supports VPC, customer-furnished KMS, audit logs, SAML/SSO and RBAC. We also provide SOC 2 artifacts and can work through any additional attestation you need.
[02:27] Sam: Good. A couple of specifics: our current SLA is 95th percentile latency under 300ms for short prompts, and cost per 1M tokens is at a baseline with OpenAI — we need to see comparable economics.
[02:39] Priya: For latency we look at model size, sequence length, and batching. For predictable sub-300ms tails we'd recommend pinning smaller model variants or using a dedicated low-latency pool. We also have quantization profiles that materially lower memory footprint and improve throughput; tradeoffs with quality are measured in eval.
[02:58] Jordan: Can you give example numbers for a 7B model versus a 70B on Dedicated? Roughly how much cost difference and latency delta?
[03:06] Priya: Rough ballpark: 7B with int8 quantization on our Dedicated runtime can often hit 20-60ms per token on modern GPU instances for single-stream latency depending on prompt length; 70B models might sit in 80-250ms per token range and need different kernel paths. In terms of cost, 7B variants can be an order of magnitude cheaper to serve per token. We'll share a cost matrix in the pricing sheet.
[03:28] Maya: What's the migration effort? Do you do model conversions for us, or is that on our engineering team?
[03:34] Alex: We offer migration support as part of Dedicated onboarding. For model conversions we can handle model packaging, quantization, and validation runs. If you have custom evals we can run those together. The typical pilot is 2-4 weeks with a small dedicated cluster.
[03:48] Sam: Security is a blocker for us. Our data is PHI-adjacent. We need clear data residency, encryption at rest, key ownership, and audit logging for access to requests. How does Redwood handle request logging and retention?
[04:02] Priya: For Dedicated, request logs can be routed to your storage or retained per your retention policy. You control keys via KMS/HSM integration. We can disable persistent logging of prompt content if required and only store minimal metadata. We'll surface audit logs for operator actions and access.
[04:20] Jordan: Do you have any case studies for healthcare customers with similar requirements?
[04:24] Alex: We have a couple of enterprise customers in regulated verticals; happy to share redacted case studies and our compliance pack after the call.
[04:32] Maya: We're also curious about model updates and rollouts. If we pin a model version and later want to upgrade, how do you handle canaries and rollbacks?
[04:40] Priya: Our console supports rollout policies: canary, A/B, percent traffic splits, and automatic fallback to previous pinned versions if quality degrades. We also support per-route model pinning and tracing.
[04:52] Jordan: For benchmarking can you reproduce our OpenAI environment? We use gpt-3.5-turbo and a few tuned prompts. We saw some drift when we tried local vLLM because tokenization differed slightly. Tokenization mismatches are a pain.
[05:04] Priya: Tokenization differences do happen. We normalize by using the same tokenizer during the benchmark and measure output stability. If you have a custom tokenizer or tokenization quirks, we'll capture that.
[05:14] Sam: On cost — if Dedicated is more expensive committed monthly, how do we justify it versus staying on OpenAI and using higher volume discounts?
[05:22] Alex: Good question. Dedicated shifts spend into reserved capacity with predictable throughput and improved tail latency; unit cost per token can be lower for sustained high throughput after you factor in batching, KV cache reuse, and lower egress costs. We can model your current usage and show a TCO comparison.
[05:36] Maya: Do you support hybrid routing? Like keep some traffic on OpenAI for certain paths and run sensitive data on Dedicated?
[05:42] Priya: Yes, smart routing is a key pattern: route by policy (latency, cost, region, or data sensitivity). We can keep a subset on hosted endpoints and route sensitive or high-volume production traffic to Dedicated.
[05:54] Jordan: Any friction around fine-tuning or RLHF? We do some finetuning workflows right now via OpenAI.
[06:01] Alex: We support model versions and hosting of fine-tuned artifacts. For proprietary finetuning pipelines we can host the resulting checkpoints and manage rollout. For RLHF pipelines you'll want to discuss data handling for training; that's typically part of a Private or on-prem engagement.
[06:14] Sam: How about observability? We need per-route latency, token counts, error rates, and traces to root cause issues.
[06:20] Priya: Redwood Console provides per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks so you can attach distributed traces, and alerts. We can also export metrics to your Prometheus/Grafana stack.
[06:33] Maya: One implementation detail: our current stack has a proxy layer that does retries and caching. Will that interfere with Redwood's batching and KV cache?
[06:41] Priya: Caching layers external to the runtime can reduce the benefits of prefix/KV cache in the serving runtime. We typically recommend letting the runtime handle prefix caching and batching for best economics; but we can work with your proxy set up. During pilot we test end-to-end including your proxy to measure real world SLOs.
[06:58] Jordan: About quantization — you mentioned int8 — we saw some quality drop on adversarial prompts. How do you validate quality post-quantization?
[07:06] Priya: We run your eval set pre and post quantization and measure exact-match, EM, F1, and custom metrics. For adversarial cases we flag regressions and can tune per-layer quantization or choose mixed-precision paths.
[07:19] Alex: Also worth noting we can keep a high-quality variant on standby and route requests to it for flagged prompts if you need guaranteed fidelity for certain flows.
[07:28] Sam: That fallback sounds useful. About timelines: if we greenlight a pilot this month what's realistic?
[07:34] Alex: Pilot typically kicks off within 1-2 weeks after contracting and infra provisioning; bench runs take 1-2 weeks. So you could be live on a trial cluster within 3-5 weeks end-to-end.
[07:45] Maya: Who's involved on Redwood's side during pilot?
[07:48] Priya: A solutions engineer for setup and benchmarking, an onboarding manager for infra provisioning, and an engineer for model packaging if needed. Alex here will coordinate.
[07:58] Jordan: A small technical question — how do you handle KV cache invalidation across instances during scaling? We saw stale KV issues in a cluster setup previously.
[08:07] Priya: Our runtime has a distributed KV cache manager and we maintain per-session caches pinned to warm workers; on autoscale we migrate caches or fall back to re-populating caches; it's not perfect but we aim to minimize cold starts with pre-warming heuristics. We log metrics around cache hit/miss and used that during tuning.
[08:28] Sam: Any hidden costs we should be aware of — egress, long-term retention, support SLAs?
[08:34] Alex: Egress is usually included in Dedicated contracts up to reasonable limits; long-term storage for logs can be an add-on. Support SLAs vary by tier — enterprise SLAs include faster response and dedicated CSMs. We'll include all specifics in the SOW.
[08:48] Maya: Okay, let's talk about parity testing more concretely. Jordan will upload a 500-prompt eval set and a few key metrics. What sample size do you recommend?
[08:58] Priya: For parity we like 500-2,000 prompts depending on variability. Include edge/adversarial cases and normal traffic. We'll run A/B comparisons: OpenAI live, Redwood Dedicated variant, and a vLLM/TGI baseline where possible.
[09:15] Jordan: Good. We'll also include some token distribution and the percent of sessions that are short (<50 tokens) vs long.
[09:21] Alex: Perfect. On the security pack we'll send SOC 2 artifacts, and Priya will attach docs for KMS integration and network diagrams.
[09:28] Sam: Last thing — what about model licensing? If we want to run a particular HF checkpoint,are there license issues?
[09:34] Priya: We review model licenses during onboarding. Some community checkpoints are permissive, others require attribution or have restrictions. We advise and handle packaging but you'll need to ensure compliance with the model license.
[09:45] Maya: Great. Let's recap next steps quickly.
[09:48] Alex: Recap: Alex to send pricing and SOW, Priya to schedule technical deep dive and benchmark, Jordan to provide prompt set and usage metrics, Sam to loop in security. We'll aim to have pilot scoped within a week.
[10:03] Sam: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:06] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.

End of transcript.
